title: Quantum Oscillations of $\mathrm{Sr}_2\mathrm{RuO}_4$ under c-Axis Uniaxial Stress
authors: Fabian Jerzembeck, Maximilian T. Pelly, Helge Rosner, Edgar Abarca Morales, Naoki Kikugawa, Dmitry A. Sokolov, Andrew P. Mackenzie, Andreas W. Rost, Elena Hassinger, Javier F. Landaeta
abstract: Uniaxial stress has now been widely used to study correlated electron materials. However, Fermi surface-resolved experimental data on the evolution of the electronic structure under piezoelectrically applied stress are sparse, with no reports of de Haas-van Alphen (dHvA) effects under uniaxial stress. Here we present dHvA measurements under $c$-axis uniaxial stress on the unconventional superconductor $\mathrm{Sr}_2\mathrm{RuO}_4$. This allows us to study the evolution of the electronic structure directly and to gain insight into the contradicting behavior of the predicted enhancement of the electronic density of states and the observed suppression of $T_\text{c}$. We are able to follow all Fermi surfaces for stress up to $-1.8$~GPa and find that the cross-sectional areas of the hole-like $α$ sheet increase and electron-like $β$ sheet decrease. At the same time, the area of the electron-like $γ$ sheet increases. Therefore, in contrast to in-plane uniaxial stress, charge transfer is the mechanism for approaching the electron-to-hole Lifshitz transition and the associated Van Hove singularity. Additionally, we find that the effective masses on all three Fermi sheets are slightly enhanced as the Lifshitz transition is approached. We compare the dHvA results with quantum oscillations in the magnetostriction and band structure calculations, and find good agreement. At a more general level, our findings show that quantum oscillation measurements under uniaxial stress, combined with band-structure calculations, offer a promising new route for studying quantum materials.
summary: This work uses dHvA measurements on $\mathrm{Sr}_2\mathrm{RuO}_4$ to map how uniaxial strain modifies its electronic structure. By observing changes in Fermi surface areas and effective masses, the authors demonstrate that stress induces charge transfer between orbital sheets, driving the system toward a Lifshitz transition. This establishes quantum oscillation measurements under mechanical stress as a powerful new experimental route for probing correlated electron physics.
main_problem: The study investigates how uniaxial stress affects the electronic structure and Fermi surface of the unconventional superconductor $\mathrm{Sr}_2\mathrm{RuO}_4$, specifically addressing discrepancies between predicted density of states enhancement and observed $T_c$ suppression.
main_result: Under c-axis compression, charge transfer occurs from hole-like to electron-like sheets ($\alpha 	o \gamma$), driving the system toward a Lifshitz transition. The measurements confirm that quantum oscillation data, combined with band structure calculations, provide a powerful new tool for studying quantum materials.
method: The research combines De Haas-van Alphen (dHvA) quantum oscillation measurements under uniaxial stress ($\sigma_{zz}$) with theoretical predictions from Density Functional Theory (DFT) and magnetostriction analysis.
model_or_system: The system is the correlated electron material $\mathrm{Sr}_2\mathrm{RuO}_4$, an unconventional superconductor. The study probes its electronic structure evolution by applying controlled uniaxial strain/stress along the c-axis, which modifies the Fermi surface topology and carrier distribution among different orbital sheets ($\alpha,  eta, \gamma$).
key_observables: dHvA frequencies (cross-sectional areas of $\alpha,  eta, \gamma$ sheets), effective masses ($m^*$), critical stress for Lifshitz transition ($\sigma_{	ext{crit},c}$), and the superconducting critical temperature $T_c$.
important_parameters: Uniaxial stress up to $-1.8$ GPa (or higher in some analyses); Fermi surface sheets $\alpha,  eta, \gamma$; Temperature dependence of quantum oscillation amplitudes.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed changes are due to intrinsic electronic structure evolution rather than experimental artifacts like strain inhomogeneity or temperature gradients; DFT calculations provide a reliable baseline for band structure predictions.
figures_summary: Figures show raw dHvA oscillations and Fourier spectra demonstrating frequency shifts under stress. Comparisons are made between these experimental results, magnetostriction measurements, and DFT-calculated frequency shifts to validate the physical mechanism of charge transfer and topology change.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for studying electronic structure evolution under strain in correlated materials. It presents dHvA measurements showing clear quantum oscillations up to high stresses. The core analysis details how Fermi surface areas change (charge transfer) and how effective masses are modified, comparing these findings rigorously against DFT calculations to pinpoint the approach toward a Lifshitz transition.
why_interesting: The methodology—using quantum oscillations under controlled strain combined with first-principles theory—is highly valuable for understanding emergent phenomena in strongly correlated systems where external tuning parameters (like stress) can drive topological phase transitions or alter superconducting pairing mechanisms.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic 2D Fermi surface of Sr2RuO4 under uniaxial stress. (a) Zero stress. (b) In-plane uniaxial stress |σxx| > |σcrit,xx|. (c) Out-of-plane uniaxial stress |σzz| > |σcrit,zz|.

Figure 2. (a) Raw dHvA oscillations as a function of magnetic field at 90 mK (stress cell temperature) for a series of compressive stresses. (b) Same data as in (a) plotted versus inverse field; curves are vertically shifted for clarity. (c–e) Fourier spectra highlighting the α, β, γ, and 2α +β peaks under different stresses. FFTs were taken over the field range 3–15 T for α and 8–15 T for the other Fermi surface sheets.

Figure 4. Comparison of the FFTs (8–15 T range) of quantum oscil- lations from magnetostriction (85 mK) and dHvA (125 mK) on the same sample. Before comparison, the strain FFT was multiplied by F2 (details are in the main text). Both spectra are then normalized to the α peak height. The inset shows the raw dilatometer signal (strain oscillations) as a function of field.

Figure 3. Lifshitz-Kosevich effective mass analysis at 0 GPa (circles, solid lines) and −1 GPa (squares, dashed lines). Uncertainties on the effective masses from the fits are estimated to be about 2% for the α and β sheets, and about 5% for the γ sheet.

Figure 6. (a) Photo of a two-part carrier: the sample is mounted across a gap (red rectangle) with an excitation coil around its neck. (b) c-axis sample with a 48 turns pick-up coil.
